notes:
I hit the research tool's usage limit early, so these notes rest on fewer sources than you asked for. I read Enduring Word (Guzik) and Ellicott in full. For Gill, the Pulpit Commentary, Spurgeon, Matthew Henry, Clarke, Calvin, Coffman, Constable and Augustine, I only saw the short excerpts the search results showed. I didn't reach netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, wesley.nnu.edu, catholic.com or oca.org. I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this psalm, so that section is left out.

## Introduction and title
- **Setting:** No one knows the occasion. Because the psalm is about flocks and grain, many think it was written for a harvest festival, perhaps the Feast of Tabernacles. Spurgeon calls the "psalm" and "song" pairing in the title a lyrical poem that can be said or sung. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-65/
- **One of Spurgeon's quoted writers** sets it in the autumn, when the year's sins had been covered at the atonement service and the harvest was in. Another of his sources sees a temple thanksgiving paying vows made during a long drought. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps065.cfm
- **Spurgeon's outline:** verses 1–4 are about approaching God, 5–8 about the wonders God does in answer to prayer, and 9–13 are a harvest song. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps065.php
- **Date and author (critical view):** Ellicott thinks the mention of the Temple rules out David as author. He notes that some date it to Sennacherib's defeat and others to the exile. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/65.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** it also doubts David wrote it, because of the temple "courts" and the style. It reads the psalm as pure praise in three stanzas. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-65.html
- **Ancient title:** The Vulgate and some Septuagint (LXX) manuscripts add that this is a song of Jeremiah and Ezekiel for the exiles about to return home. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/65.htm
- **Augustine (Catholic and Orthodox church father)** takes that title as prophecy. He treats exile in Babylon and earthly Jerusalem as pictures, with Jerusalem standing for the everlasting city in heaven. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801065.htm

## v. 1
- **"Praise awaits":** the Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "be silent." Morgan says the praise is so full it can't find words at first. Kidner says falling silent in awe can be the height of worship. Guzik pictures praise ready to greet God when he meets his people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-65/
- **Ellicott** finds "praise is silence to you" hard to make sense of. He suggests "to you belong quiet and praise": quiet waiting until deliverance comes, then joyful praise. He notes the LXX and Vulgate read "praise is fitting." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/65.htm
- **Spurgeon's notes** read it as patient, untroubled waiting, like tuning a harp before the good news comes. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps065.cfm
- **Spurgeon's exposition** pictures praise waiting for the King to appear, like musicians waiting for a prince. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps065.php
- **Matthew Henry** cites the Aramaic paraphrase (the Targum): before God, praise counts as silence. He says praise waits for God in Zion, meaning his church and people. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_065.cfm
- **Clarke (Methodist)** says all other perfections are lost in God's, so he alone is worthy of praise. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-65.html
- **Vows:** People came to Jerusalem to give thanks and pay their vows. Guzik counts baptism as a vow. Spurgeon warns that an unkept vow burns the conscience. Guzik also sees Christ, the Son of David, keeping the greatest vow at Zion. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-65/
- **Ellicott** renders it "the vow is paid," meaning by this very praise. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/65.htm

## v. 2
- **Hearing prayer:** Because God hears prayer, he draws "all flesh," not Israel only. Guzik says this idea is developed later in the psalm. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-65/
- **Pulpit Commentary:** hearing prayer is a necessary attribute of God. It cites Calvin: God can no more stop hearing prayer than stop existing. Against Ewald and Hitzig, who limited "all flesh" to Israel, it argues verses 5 and 8 show the writer includes all humanity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/65.htm
- **Ellicott** accepts the usual reading, a prophecy of the faith spreading to the Gentiles. But he says the psalmist's own meaning was narrower: praise is Israel's privilege, while every nation may come to God in prayer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/65.htm
- **Clarke** also notes that this is taken as a prediction of the Gentiles' calling. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-65.html
- **Constable:** people will pray because God answers, and will fall silent before him out of respect. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/65-2.html
- **One writer quoted in Spurgeon's notes** reads "God in Zion" as, in New Testament terms, God in Christ. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps065.cfm

## v. 3
- **Atonement God provides:** David admits his sins sometimes win, and trusts God to provide the atonement. Guzik says David looked past animal sacrifices to the Messiah's perfect sacrifice on the cross. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-65/
- **Whose sins?** Ellicott reads the "me" as Israel confessing through the poet. He notes the LXX and Vulgate have a plural pronoun. He suggests "iniquity" is the frailty common to all people and "transgressions" is breaking the covenant, both purged by sacrifice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/65.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary** also thinks the nation's sins are mainly in view. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/65.htm
- **Spurgeon's notes** say David means his own sins, yet by faith sees God removing them. One writer there says God purges sin in two ways that always go together, the first being pardoning mercy. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps065.cfm
- **Clarke** says the King James wording "iniquities prevail against me" is not an accurate rendering of the Hebrew. The excerpt I saw cuts off there. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-65.html

## v. 4 (where traditions differ)
- **Guzik (Calvary Chapel / charismatic):** God causes the relationship, choosing a person and bringing them near. Some think a priest is meant. Poole notes that the "courts" were the part of the temple ordinary people could enter. Horne applies it ultimately to Christ, the chosen High Priest. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-65/
- **Spurgeon's notes (Baptist, Reformed):** we are chosen for Christ's sake and accepted in him, not on our own account. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps065.cfm
- **Ellicott (Anglican):** the chosen one is Israel, restored to covenant privilege. He suggests the Hebrew may read "he whom you choose shall dwell." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/65.htm
- **Coffman:** probably the choice of Israel as the people who would bring the Messiah, though the words apply without limit. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/65-2.html
- **In short:** the Reformed and Baptist voices stress individual election in Christ, while Ellicott and Coffman stress corporate Israel. I found no Methodist, Lutheran or Pentecostal source discussing election in this verse.
- **God as host:** Maclaren pictures a guest in God's house, safe and provided for. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-65/
- **Matthew Henry** says God keeps a good house, with plenty of grace for everyone and all of it free. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_065.cfm
- **Wording:** Ellicott suggests "let us be refreshed" and "the holiness of your temple." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/65.htm

## v. 5
- **Guzik:** confidence that God will keep answering. His reach is the whole earth, including the farthest and hardest to reach. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-65/
- **Ellicott:** "awesome deeds" works as "wondrously," and "you answer" describes God's usual way. The LXX and Vulgate make it a prayer: "hear us." He takes "ends of the earth" in its widest sense: knowingly or not, the whole world rests on God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/65.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** awesome acts of righteous judgment on Israel's enemies. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/65.htm
- **Calvin:** God preserves his church with awesome majesty, which gives hope in desperate times. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/65-5.html
- **Gill (Baptist, Calvinist):** these "terrible things" are not afflictions, because nobody prays for afflictions, so they can't be answers to prayer. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/65-5.html
- **Spurgeon's notes:** when God rescues by awesome means, he does nothing that isn't righteous. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps065.cfm

## v. 6
- **Ellicott:** God as builder, belted for work in Eastern style, setting the mountains firm. He thinks the poet also has in mind that empires owe their stability to God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/65.htm
- **Spurgeon** (quoted by Guzik) criticises thinkers so caught up in laws of geology that they forget the one who raised the mountains. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-65/

## v. 7
- **Seas and nations:** God quiets both, and Guzik says this should strengthen faith amid world turmoil. VanGemeren notes that pagan myth saw the sea as chaos, but Israel knew the Lord rules it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-65/
- **Ellicott:** the literal raging sea becomes a picture of human anarchy, compare Isaiah 17:12. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/65.htm

## v. 8
- **"Wonders" (KJV "tokens"):** Gill lists three readings: signs of God's judgment, the sun, moon and stars, and miracles of the early gospel age. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/65-8.html
- **Clarke** points to storms, eclipses and earthquakes, which show even distant peoples there is a Supreme Being. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/65-8.html
- **Dawn and sunset:** Ellicott reads this as sunrise and sunset, east and west, singing for joy, as the morning stars did in Job 38:7. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/65.htm
- **Kidner** allows either day and night or the whole earth from east to west. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-65/
- **Matthew Henry:** morning light and evening rest are both welcome gifts. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_065.cfm

## v. 9
- **"River of God":** Ellicott says it means rain, and he cites a rabbinic saying that God keeps the key of rain himself. He corrects the KJV to "you prepare their grain when you have prepared the land." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/65.htm
- **Luther**, cited via Spurgeon, calls God the real farmer who keeps tending the land while the farmer sleeps. Boice notes that rain meant life or death. Guzik: the earth is barren until God acts, and the same goes for the church. He links this to Isaiah 55:10–11. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-65/
- **Spurgeon** applies it spiritually to people made rich by grace. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps065.cfm

## v. 10
- **Ellicott:** the KJV terms should be swapped. It is the ridges between the furrows that get pressed down and softened. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/65.htm
- **Gill (allegorical):** ridges are proud people humbled by grace, furrows are humble souls God fills, and showers soften the hard heart through his Word and Spirit. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/65-10.html
- **Spurgeon** preached a sermon on the last clause, "Spring in the Heart" (No. 675). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/tod/psalms/65.htm

## v. 11
- **Clarke** (via Guzik): a full harvest is the year's crown, given by God's undeserved goodness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-65/
- **Ellicott:** "crown" first meant "encircle," so the whole year is surrounded by goodness. "Paths" may be the wheel-tracks of God's cloud-chariot. More likely it means the seasons turning. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/65.htm
- **Spurgeon** preached a sermon on this verse, "Thanksgiving and Prayer" (No. 532). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/tod/psalms/65.htm

## v. 12
- **Clarke:** even uncultivated land gets enough moisture for grazing. Gill applies the wilderness to the Gentile world watered by the gospel, and the hills to the churches. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/65-12.html
- **Clarke** (via Guzik) explains "the hills gird themselves with joy" as lambs leaping and shepherds dancing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-65/
- **Ellicott:** new plants clothe the hills like a festival cloak. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/65.htm

## v. 13
- **Gill:** the flocks may stand for many converts joining the church (Isaiah 60:7), and the valleys for humble, fruitful souls. He notes that the Targum and LXX read it as rams mating with the flocks. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/65-13.html
- **Kidner** praises the picture of hills and fields dressed up and celebrating. Spurgeon says nature's voice is a song, not just a shout. Guzik adds that God's people have even more reason to praise, because of the atonement in verses 3–4. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-65/
